name: Calendula (pot marigold)
habitat: Gardens, escaped onto waste ground and old fields; grown widely, self-seeds readily, and flowers late into the year.
identify: Bright orange to yellow daisy-like flower heads, 4-7 cm across, on soft slightly sticky stems.
Leaves are pale green, soft, oblong, slightly sticky and aromatic, clasping the stem.
Seeds are curved and warty like tiny claws — a distinctive check.
It is a Calendula, not a Tagetes 'French marigold' — the tell is the soft hairy sticky foliage and the curved seed.

lookalikes.name: French / African marigold
lookalikes.danger: Low, but they are a different plant with a different and much more pungent smell and none of the same tradition.
lookalikes.tell: Tagetes has finely divided fern-like leaves and a strong sharp scent; calendula has simple oblong leaves and a resinous sticky feel.

preparations.method: Pack DRIED flower heads into oil and leave warm for two weeks, or heat gently for a few hours; strain.
preparations.for_use: The base for a salve for grazes, chapping, nappy rash and minor burns. Dry the flowers first — water in fresh flowers spoils the oil.

preparations.method: Steep flower heads in hot water 10 minutes and cool.
preparations.for_use: A wash or compress for inflamed skin and grazes.

cautions: Asteraceae family: cross-reacts with ragweed, chrysanthemum and daisy allergies.
It supports minor skin healing. It does nothing for a deep or infected wound.
evidence: Approved for topical inflammation by the German Commission E, with several small trials for radiation dermatitis and wound healing. Among the better-supported skin herbs here.
